1.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֞ע שְׁפַטְיָ֣ה בֶן־מַתָּ֗ן וּ⁠גְדַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן־פַּשְׁח֔וּר וְ⁠יוּכַל֙ בֶּן־שֶׁ֣לֶמְיָ֔הוּ וּ⁠פַשְׁח֖וּר בֶּן־מַלְכִּיָּ֑ה
1.note: The words **Shephatiah**, **Mattan**, **Gedaliah**, **Pashhur**, **Jucal**, **Shelemiah**, and **Malkijah** are the names of men.

2.note: See how you translated this expression in 2:5.
See how you translated **The one dwelling in this city** in 21:9.

Here, **the sword** represents “war” or “being attacked by enemy soldiers.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in battle] or [from being attacked by enemy soldiers]

Yahweh is using **going out to the Chaldeans** as a common expression of the culture to mean “surrendering to the Chaldeans.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But the one surrendering to the Chaldeans will live]
See how you translated the similar phrase in Jeremiah 21:9.
See how you translated this name in 35:11. This also occurs in verses 18, 19, and 23.

3.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **given** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [This city will surely be given]

The expression **will be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that Yahweh is the one who will do the action. Alternate translation: [I will give this city]

Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under the control of the army of the king of Babylon]

4.note: The expression **let this man be put to death** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The officials are asking the king to have his men do the action. Alternate translation: [Please have your men put this man to death]

The officials are saying what they want the king to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Please order this man to be put to death]

The phrase translated as **for on account of this** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because in this way]

Jeremiah is using **he is weakening the hands of the men of war** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is causing the soldiers to lose their courage.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is taking the strength out of the soldiers’ hearts] or [he is discouraging the soldiers]

4.q: כִּ֣י הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה אֵינֶ֨⁠נּוּ דֹרֵ֧שׁ לְ⁠שָׁל֛וֹם לָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה כִּ֥י אִם־לְ⁠רָעָֽה
4.note: If your language does not use nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **evil**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [For this man is not seeking for this people to be well, but rather for them to be harmed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:10.
See how you translated the similar expression in 16:15. This also occurs in verse 6.

If your language does not use nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **harm**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [for this people to be safe but rather for them to be hurt]

5.note: Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he is under your control]

Zedekiah is speaking of himself in the third person as **the king**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for I as king am not able]

Zedekiah is using **to do a word against you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do anything against you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is not able to do anything against you]

6.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the officials who asked the king to put Jeremiah to death. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the officials took]
The word **Malkijah** is the name of a man.

7.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֡ע עֶֽבֶד־מֶ֨לֶךְ הַ⁠כּוּשִׁ֜י אִ֣ישׁ סָרִ֗יס וְ⁠הוּא֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּֽי־נָתְנ֥וּ אֶֽת־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ אֶל־הַ⁠בּ֑וֹר וְ⁠הַ⁠מֶּ֥לֶךְ יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּ⁠שַׁ֥עַר בִּנְיָמִֽן
7.note: Jeremiah is using the clause that begins with **And** to describe what Ebed Melech heard. This provides the background for the events he describes in the next verse, where this sentence continues. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing the background for what happens next. Alternate translation: [Now Ebed Melech the Cushite court official who served in the house of the king, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern. During this time, the king was sitting in the Gate of Benjamin]

7.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֡ע עֶֽבֶד־מֶ֨לֶךְ הַ⁠כּוּשִׁ֜י אִ֣ישׁ סָרִ֗יס וְ⁠הוּא֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ
7.note: Here the author is introducing Ebed Melech the Cushite as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now there was a man named Ebed Melech the Cushite court official who served in the house of the king. When he heard]
The words **Ebed Melech** are the name of a man. The word **Cushite** indicates that he was from the land of Cush. This also occurs in verses 10 and 12.

8.q: וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֥א עֶֽבֶד־מֶ֖לֶךְ מִ⁠בֵּ֣ית הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ
8.note: The implication is that Ebed Melech went to the Gate of Benjamin, where the king was sitting, in order to speak with him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Ebed Melech went out from the house of the king to the Gate of Benjamin, where the king was sitting, and spoke to him saying,]

9.note: Ebed Melech is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no more food]

Ebed Melech is using **from the face of the hunger** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of the hunger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the hunger]

10.note: Zedekiah is using **Take in your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Take with you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take along 30 men from here]

11.note: Jeremiah is using **took the men in his hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “took the men with him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Ebed Melech took the men along]

The implication is that Ebed Melech went to a room that was **under the storehouse**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to a room below the storehouse]
See how you translated the similar expression in 35:12. This also occurs in verses 12, 14, 16, 19, 24, and 27.

12.note: The implication is that the rags and clothes would serve as padding between Jeremiah’s armpits and the ropes, so that the ropes would not hurt him as the men pulled him up. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [under the ropes so that the ropes will not hurt you when the men pull you up]

13.note: The implication is that Jeremiah was still a prisoner who was being guarded there. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jeremiah remained a prisoner under guard in the courtyard of the guard]

14.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֞ח הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ צִדְקִיָּ֗הוּ וַ⁠יִּקַּ֞ח אֶֽת־יִרְמְיָ֤הוּ הַ⁠נָּבִיא֙ אֵלָ֔י⁠ו
14.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And King Zedekiah sent messengers, and they took Jeremiah the prophet to the king]

Here, **a word** represents “a question” or “a matter.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I am going to ask you a question]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:26.

15.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that he is sure Zedekiah would put him to death. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you will surely put me to death!]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **putting to death** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will you not surely put me to death]

16.note: See how you translated this phrase in 5:2.
See how you translated “into the hand of” in 12:7.

Zedekiah is using **seeking your life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “trying to kill you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [these men who want to kill you]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:14.

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **go out** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [If you really do go out]

Yahweh is using **your soul** to represent Zedekiah himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 20. Alternate translation: [then you yourself will live]

The expression **will not be burned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that the Chaldeans are the ones who would do the action. Alternate translation: [and the Chaldeans will not burn this city with fire]
See how you translated the similar phrase “going out” in 38:2. Alternate translation: [you obey my warning and surrender]

Here, **your house** represents “your family” or “your household.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you and your household]

18.note: The expression **will be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that Yahweh is the one who will do the action. Alternate translation: [then I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans]
See how you translated the similar expression in 22:25.

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will not escape** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the certainty of what will happen king Zedekiah. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [and as for you, you will not escape]
See how you translated “into the hand of” in 12:7. Alternate translation: [from their power]

19.note: King Zedekiah is using **who have fallen away** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who have deserted.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

The first **they** refers to the Chaldeans, while **their** and the second **they** refer to the Judeans who have fallen away to the Chaldeans. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [lest the Chaldeans give me into the hand of those Judeans and those Judeans deal ruthlessly with me]
See how you translated the similar phrase in 12:7.

20.note: Here, **voice** represents “what Yahweh says.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Listen, please, to the message of Yahweh]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The Babylonians will not give you over to the Judeans]

Here, **that** marks **it may go well for you, and your soul may live** as the goal or purpose of **Listen, please, to the voice of Yahweh, to what I am speaking to you**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

21.note: Here, **the word** represents “the message” that Yahweh revealed to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is the message that Yahweh has shown me]

22.q: כָל־הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר נִשְׁאֲרוּ֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֔ה מוּצָא֕וֹת אֶל־שָׂרֵ֖י מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֑ל
22.note: The expression **are being brought out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to state who will do the action, you could say that it is the enemy soldiers. Alternate translation: [the enemy soldiers are bringing out all the women who are left in the house of the king of Judah to the officials of the king of Babylon]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the men of your peace** before the information about what they did to Zedekiah. Alternate translation: [The men of your peace have incited you and have prevailed over you]

The women are using **the men of your peace** as a common expression of the culture to mean “your trusted friends.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the friends you relied on]

Here the women are speaking as if Zedekiah were a man whose feet were stuck in **the mire** and whose friends had left him there. It means that he is helpless and that the friends he trusted have abandoned him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You cannot get yourself out of trouble, and your friends have deserted you]

23.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:30.

The pronoun **they** refers to the enemy soldiers who will capture the city. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the enemy soldiers are bringing out all your wives and your sons to the Chaldeans]

Here, the pronoun **you** is stated separately, even though the verb translated as **you will not escape** already includes this meaning. Jeremiah is doing that to emphasize that King Zedekiah himself, in addition to his wives and sons, will not escape. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and you yourself will not escape]

Here, **hand** represents the power of the king of Babylon, who will act through his soldiers. See how you translated “into the hand of” in 12:7.
 Alternate translation: [from being captured by them, for the soldiers of the king of Babylon will seize you]

The expression **you will be seized** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that the king of Babylon will do the action through his soldiers. Alternate translation: [for the king of Babylon will seize you through his soldiers] or [the soldiers of the king of Babylon will seize you]

24.note: See how you translated this expression in 12:15.

By **and you will not die**, Zedekiah means that if Jeremiah keeps their conversation secret, the officials will have no reason to kill him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the officials will not kill you]

25.q: וְ⁠כִֽי־יִשְׁמְע֣וּ הַ⁠שָּׂרִים֮ כִּֽי־דִבַּ֣רְתִּי אִתָּ⁠ךְ֒ וּ⁠בָ֣אוּ אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ וְֽ⁠אָמְר֪וּ אֵלֶ֟י⁠ךָ
25.note: Zedekiah is presenting a possible condition, that the officials might hear that he has spoken with Jeremiah and come to question him. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Zedekiah states what Jeremiah should do in that case in the next verse. Alternate translation: [But suppose the officials hear that I have spoken with you, and they come to you and say to you]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you should please declare to them what you spoke to the king]

26.note: Jeremiah is using **causing my supplication to fall to the face of ** as a common expression of the culture to mean “humbly pleading with.” See how you translated the similar expression “Perhaps their supplication will fall to the face of” in 36:7. Alternate translation: [I myself am humbly pleading with the king]

27.note: The expression **had not been heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that no one besides Zedekiah and Jeremiah had heard what they said to each other. Alternate translation: [for no one else had heard the matter]

28.q: עַד־י֖וֹם אֲשֶׁר־נִלְכְּדָ֣ה יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠הָיָ֕ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִלְכְּדָ֖ה יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
28.note: The expression **was captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that the Babylonians are the ones who captured it. Alternate translation: [until the day that the Babylonians captured Jerusalem. And he was there when the Babylonians captured Jerusalem]
